intuition: Each input list is sorted, so its first remaining node has its smallest remaining value. Compare those two nodes and attach the smaller one to the result. Repeat until one list ends, then attach the rest of the other list.

The output tail marks the last node already chosen. A dummy node gives that tail an initial home before any real node has been selected, avoiding a separate first-node branch. After attaching a node, advance the pointer for the input it came from and then advance the output tail.

When one input becomes empty, the other suffix needs no more comparisons. It is already sorted, and every value in it is at least the last selected value. Splicing this suffix onto the tail finishes the merge without allocating replacement nodes. Equal values may come from either input; both original nodes still have to appear.

steps: Begin with list1=1→2→4 and list2=1→3→4, with tail pointing to the dummy.
The two heads tie at 1. Select list1’s first node, leaving its next head at 2.
Compare 2 with list2’s 1; select that second 1. Next select 2 before 3.
Select 3, then select list1’s 4 when the two remaining heads tie.
List1 is now exhausted. Attach list2’s final 4 and return dummy.next, yielding 1→1→2→3→4→4.

codeNotes.note: The dummy is an output anchor, not a value included in the answer. It makes empty-input cases follow the same control flow.
Relinking preserves the selected input node rather than copying its value into a replacement node.
The remaining suffix is already ordered, so a single link completes all remaining work.

keyDecision: Choose the smaller current head. Move only the pointer for the list you chose.

intuition: Sorting every node again ignores the order already present in the two lists. The smallest remaining node of each list is always its head, so deeper nodes cannot be the next result while that head remains.

Imagine two ordered queues feeding one output chain. Compare their exposed front values and attach the smaller front node. Only that queue advances. When a queue empties, its counterpart’s remaining chain is already correctly ordered.

approach: Compare the first remaining node of each list.
Attach the smaller node and expose its successor.
When one list ends, attach the rest of the other list.
concept.correctness: Every time a node is attached, it is no larger than either list’s remaining head and hence no larger than any remaining node. The output therefore stays sorted. Advancing only its source uses every original node once. When one list empties, the other suffix is already ordered and belongs after the completed prefix.

complexity.explanation: Each node is attached once, so work is proportional to the combined list lengths. Reusing the original nodes requires only a few bookmarks and one temporary starting node.

pitfalls: Advance the chosen source and the output tail.
Return the first real output node.
